messages.content: Maintain a 2:1 ratio of declarative to interrogative sentences in your response. Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
The setting is a metric space M.
Is M complete?
If M is complete, then for any nested nonempty closed sets F_n with F_{n+1} subset F_n and diam F_n tending to 0 and any choice of points x_n in F_n, the sequence (x_n) is Cauchy because d(x_m,x_n) <= diam F_n for m>n.
Completeness gives a point x with x_n tending to x, and since the tail of (x_n) from index k onward lies in F_k, closedness forces x into every F_k, so the intersection is nonempty.
What happens in the converse direction?
For a Cauchy sequence (y_n), the sets F_n can be defined as the closures of {y_k: k>=n}.
These F_n are nonempty closed, nested, and their diameters tend to 0 because Cauchy tails have arbitrarily small diameter and closures preserve diameters, so the assumed intersection property yields x in their intersection.
Does this complete the argument?
Because y_n is in F_n and x is in F_n, the distance d(x,y_n) is at most diam F_n, which tends to 0, so M is complete.
